publisher: Sennrich, Haddow, Birch, University of Edinburgh
title: BPE subword tokenization: splitting words into common pieces so a fixed vocabulary can spell any word — the origin of LLM tokens
summary: Neural translation models had vocabularies of only tens of thousands of words, so rare and new words were untranslatable. This paper turns the 1994 byte pair encoding compression algorithm into a tokenization method: start from letters and repeatedly merge the most common neighboring pair. We work through 10 merges from the paper's code, then look at its experiments, the errors that inconsistent segmentation causes, and how this became the token in today's LLMs.
ai_summary: "Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units" (Sennrich et al., University of Edinburgh, ACL 2016) uses byte pair encoding (BPE) for word segmentation: start from characters and repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent symbol pair in the corpus into a new symbol; the number of merges sets the vocabulary size. Rare and new words are represented as sequences of subword units, so the translation model no longer needs a back-off dictionary. On the WMT 2015 English-to-German and English-to-Russian tasks, subword models beat the dictionary baseline by up to 1.1 and 1.3 BLEU; rare-word translation clearly improves, and BPE learned jointly over both languages segments more consistently.
brief: The problem: translation models had vocabularies of only tens of thousands of words. Rare words, names, and compounds could only be handled by dictionary lookup or copying, and the model couldn't generate new words.
The method: borrow the BPE compression algorithm, start from letters, repeatedly merge the most common adjacent pair, and use a fixed vocabulary to represent any word.
The result: no dictionary needed—English-to-German and English-to-Russian BLEU rise by up to 1.1 and 1.3 points, rare and unseen words translate better, and joint BPE segments more consistently.
The limits: vocabulary size is set by trial and error; character bigrams, not BPE, reach the highest BLEU; separate BPEs can segment inconsistently and cause transliteration errors.

cover.headline: A close read of the original BPE subword tokenization paper
cover.highlight: A fixed vocabulary that can spell any word

nodes.label: Repeatedly merging the most common pair

sections.h: The short version: what this paper actually did

blocks.p: In August 2015, Rico Sennrich, Barry Haddow, and Alexandra Birch at the University of Edinburgh released this paper; it was published the following year at ACL 2016. It targets an old problem in neural machine translation: **the model's vocabulary is fixed, but the words it needs to translate are not**.

Neural translation models at the time typically had a vocabulary of only 30,000 to 50,000 words. Everything outside that became an “unknown word” symbol, patched up at translation time by a dictionary lookup or by copying the word as is. But names, compounds, loanwords, and newly coined words keep appearing—especially in a language like German, which can stack several words into one long one.

The paper's answer: **break words into smaller “subwords.”** Common words stay whole; rare words split into a few common pieces, or down to single letters if necessary. A fixed-size vocabulary can then represent any word. How? The paper borrows a 1994 data compression algorithm, **byte pair encoding** (Byte Pair Encoding, BPE): start from single letters and repeatedly merge the two symbols that most often appear next to each other in the corpus. The number of merges decides the vocabulary size.

On the WMT 2015 English-to-German and English-to-Russian tasks, subword models no longer need dictionary lookups. They beat the dictionary baseline by up to 1.1 and 1.3 BLEU points respectively, and they translate rare words—and words never seen in training—considerably better.

The paper's influence reaches far beyond machine translation. When today's large models like GPT and LLaMA talk about **tokens**, most of those tokens are produced by BPE or a variant. The idea behind “a model reads one token at a time” took shape here.

callout.title: In one sentence
callout.text: BPE = start from letters and repeatedly glue the most common adjacent pair into one unit. Common words eventually become a single unit; rare words stay as a few pieces. That is how a fixed-size vocabulary can spell any word.

callout.title: Three concepts you need before reading
callout.text: Don't worry if you haven't seen them before; these three are enough:
list: **Vocabulary**: the list of all symbols a model knows. The size of the model's input and output layers is proportional to vocabulary size, so the vocabulary cannot be infinitely large.
**Encoder-decoder translation model**: one network reads the source text, another writes the translation, and attention aligns the two. This is the model from our deep read of “Bahdanau attention.”
**BLEU**: measures how much the machine translation overlaps with reference translations. Higher is better.

sections.h: The problem: a closed vocabulary, an open language

blocks.p: Word-level translation models handle out-of-vocabulary words—OOV in the paper's terms—by “backing off to a dictionary.” The model first emits an unknown-word symbol, then uses attention to find the corresponding source word, looks it up in a bilingual dictionary, and copies it as is when the lookup fails.

The paper points out several problems. Words in two languages don't always correspond one to one—a single German compound can correspond to several English words. Copying is reasonable for names, but many cases require morphological changes or transliteration, such as turning Latin letters into Cyrillic. And a word-level model simply **cannot generate** new words that were not in training.
But many “unknown words” are actually **transparently translatable**: a competent translator can produce them on first sight from their parts. The paper gives three types:

fig.subtitle: Examples from Section 3 of the paper.
rows: English Barack Obama → Russian Барак Обама
If the alphabets match, copy; if they differ, transliterate.
Change a few letters by regular rules
English solar system → German Sonnensystem (Sonne + System)
Split into morphemes, translate each separately, then reassemble

blocks.p: The paper counts 100 rare tokens in the German training data—words not among the 50,000 most frequent types—and finds that most can be translated from English this way: 56 compounds, 21 names, 6 loanwords with a common origin, 5 words with transparent affixation, plus 1 number and 1 computer language identifier.

sections.h: BPE: turning a compression algorithm into a segmentation algorithm

blocks.p: Original BPE was a compression algorithm proposed by Gage in 1994: repeatedly find the most frequent pair of bytes in the data and replace it with an unused byte. The paper moves this to word segmentation, merging characters or character sequences instead of bytes:

list: **Initialize**: start with a vocabulary containing only the individual characters. Write each word as a character sequence and append a special end-of-word symbol (written as · in the paper and `</w>` in the code) so word boundaries can be restored after translation.

**Count**: count every adjacent symbol pair. Each word is weighted by its frequency in the corpus, and pairs never cross word boundaries, so the counting only has to run over a “word → frequency” dictionary and is fast.
**Merge**: replace the most frequent pair—say A and B—with a new symbol AB everywhere it occurs, and add AB to the vocabulary.
**Repeat**: go back to the counting step until the preset number of merges is reached.

blocks.p: Every merge produces a new symbol that represents a character sequence. Common character sequences—even whole common words—eventually become single symbols. The final vocabulary size equals the initial character count plus the number of merges, and **the number of merges is the algorithm's only hyperparameter**.

At test time, split a new word into characters, then apply the learned merge rules **in the order they were learned**. This works for any word, so the vocabulary is fixed but the words it can represent are open. The paper says the only possible unknown symbols are characters never seen in training.

callout.title: Like finding common collocations in a text
callout.text: BPE is a little like abridging a book: first you notice that “t” is most often followed by “h,” so you treat “th” as a unit; then “th” is most often followed by “e,” so you create “the.” High-frequency combinations keep sticking together until a whole common word becomes one unit. Low-frequency words never stick together and remain as parts. It knows no grammar—only statistics.

blocks.p: The paper includes a Python implementation of only a dozen or so lines. Let's run its example:

quiz.q: What is the only BPE hyperparameter you set by hand?
options: The number of merges, which directly sets the final vocabulary size.
The maximum number of pieces per word
How the end-of-word symbol is written
quiz.why: Final vocabulary = initial characters + one new symbol per merge. More merges mean larger common pieces and shorter text, but a larger vocabulary. The paper's English-to-German experiments use 59,500 merges.

sections.h: The trade-off between vocabulary size and text length

blocks.p: A segmentation method has to balance two forces. A larger vocabulary makes the model's input and output layers larger, slower, and more memory-hungry. A too-small vocabulary forces each word into many pieces, lengthening the sequence; encoder and decoder computation is at least linear in sequence length, and the model must pass information across longer distances.

fig.title: The same German training corpus, segmented different ways
fig.subtitle: From Table 1 of the paper. Token counts are in millions; “unknown” is the number of tokens in the development set that cannot be segmented.
fig.note: Whole words require 1.75 million entries and still don't cover everything. Single characters leave no unknown words, but the text becomes more than 5 times longer. BPE grows the text by only about 12%, shrinks the vocabulary to just over 60,000, and has no unknown words.

blocks.p: The paper also tries linguistic methods: frequency-based compound splitting, rule-based syllable splitting, and unsupervised morpheme segmentation with Morfessor. These only shrink the vocabulary moderately and still don't solve unknown words, so they miss the goal of an open vocabulary without a dictionary.

sections.h: Two languages: learn BPE separately or jointly?

blocks.p: Translation involves two languages, so BPE can be learned separately on the source and target sides, or learned once on the combined data from both languages—what the paper calls **joint BPE**.

list: **Learned separately**: text and vocabulary are more compact, and it guarantees that every piece appeared in that language's training text.

**Learned jointly**: segmentation is more consistent across the two sides. With separate BPE, the same name can be split differently in the two languages, making it hard for the model to learn the mapping between the pieces.

blocks.p: How do you learn joint BPE when English and Russian use different alphabets? The paper first transliterates the Russian side into Latin characters using ISO-9, learns BPE on the combined corpus, then transliterates the learned merge operations back into Cyrillic and applies them to the Russian text.

The experiments use WMT 2015 data: the English-to-German training set has 4.2 million sentence pairs, about 100 million tokens; English-to-Russian has 2.6 million sentence pairs, about 50 million tokens. The model follows the Bahdanau et al. encoder-decoder architecture, with a hidden layer size of 1000, an embedding layer size of 620, training with Adadelta for about 7 days, and a beam size of 12. Each setting trains 8 models; the paper reports the best single model on the development set and an ensemble of all 8.

Systems compared: WUnk (a word-level model that emits an unknown symbol for out-of-vocabulary words), WDict (word-level model + back-off dictionary, the main baseline), C2-50k (the 50,000 most frequent words stay whole; the rest are split into character bigrams), BPE-60k (separate BPE per language), and BPE-J90k (joint BPE). None of the subword systems use a back-off dictionary.

fig.title: English-to-German: subword models translate rare and unseen words better
fig.subtitle: From Table 2 of the paper, newstest2015, ensemble of 8 models. BLEU and chrF3: higher is better; the “rare words” and “unseen words” columns are unigram F1 (%).
fig.note: Rare words are words not among the 50,000 most frequent in the training data; unseen words are words that never appeared in training. In English-to-German, most unseen words are names, where copying is correct, so the dictionary baseline actually does best in this column.

fig.title: English-to-Russian: when alphabets differ, the subword advantage is clearer
fig.subtitle: From Table 3 of the paper, newstest2015, ensemble of 8 models.
fig.note: Russian uses Cyrillic, so names cannot be copied; they must be transliterated. The dictionary baseline has an unseen-word F1 of only 6.6, while subword models learn to transliterate piece by piece and lift it to 18.3.

blocks.p: Several observations: every subword system has a higher rare-word F1 than the baseline—English-to-German goes from 36.8% to 41.8%, English-to-Russian from 26.5% to 29.7%. Ensemble BLEU beats the baseline by 0.3 to 1.3 points, and joint BPE is better than separate BPE on most metrics. The paper also cautions that rare words are only a small share of the test set, but they often carry the core information of a sentence, so overall metrics like BLEU likely understate their impact.

**Frequency analysis.** The paper groups translated words by their frequency rank in the training set. For the 50,000 most frequent words, all systems perform about the same. For words ranked between 50,000 and 500,000, whole-word representations degrade sharply as frequency falls, while subword systems stay much more stable. The reason is sparsity: the word ranked 50,000 appears only 60 times, and the word ranked 500,000 appears only 2 times, so they can never be learned well; subword pieces are far more common. So **shrinking the vocabulary and representing more words as subwords can actually be better**.

fig.title: How subword models translate words they have never seen
fig.subtitle: From Tables 4 and 5 of the paper. “|” marks subword boundaries.

list: **A “wrong” segmentation can still translate correctly.** BPE segmentation does not always respect morpheme boundaries. For example, BPE-60k splits the word for “research institutes” into `Forsch|ungsinstitu|ten`, although `Forschungs|instituten` is linguistically more natural—and the translation is still correct. The character-bigram system cuts the same word into more than a dozen pieces and also translates that part correctly (though its output also drops health). The paper says the model is robust to over-splitting.

**Inconsistent segmentation causes errors.** Separately learned BPE-60k transliterates `rakfisk` with an extra `п` and a missing `к`. The paper traces this to training examples where the two sides segment differently—for instance, `p|rak|ri|ti` corresponds to `пра|крит|и`—so the model wrongly learns `rak → пра`. Joint BPE keeps the segmentation consistent and avoids the problem.

**With too little data, transliteration can go wrong**: asinine (“stupid”) should have been translated as dumm, but the subword model produced something like Asinin-Situation—wrong, but a plausible guess for a loanword.

**The opening example is misspelled**: the paper opens with the German compound Abwasser|behandlungs|anlange (“sewage treatment plant”), but the correct spelling is Abwasserbehandlungsanlage—the last segment has an extra n.

**Figure 1 and the code use different examples**: Algorithm 1's code runs on low, lower, newest, widest, but Figure 1 shows merges learned from low, lowest, newer, wider. The text's claim that the unseen word “lower” is segmented into “low er·” refers to the Figure 1 example. Running the code directly will not reproduce Figure 1.

**The “9–11%” doesn't match the tables**: the text says rare words make up 9% to 11% of the test set. Based on the word counts in Tables 2 and 3, English-to-German is 2900 / 44085, about 6.6%, and English-to-Russian is 5442 / 55654, about 9.8%. The discrepancy may come from a different counting method, but the paper doesn't say.

**The best BLEU is not from BPE**: the highest English-to-German ensemble BLEU (25.3) comes from the character-bigram system; BPE-60k's single-model BLEU (21.5) is even below the dictionary baseline (22.0). The paper's main evidence is rare-word F1 and chrF3, not BLEU.

**Vocabulary size is chosen by feel**: the paper admits the number of merges was chosen “somewhat arbitrarily,” mainly for comparability with prior work; automatically finding the optimal vocabulary size is left for future research.

sections.h: Afterward: how today's LLM tokens came to be

blocks.p: BPE quickly became the standard first step for processing text in neural networks. Several papers in Main Thread 1 show it in action:

fig.title: How the models in Main Thread 1 split text
fig.subtitle: From each paper's data processing section
rows: BPE, with one shared vocabulary for source and target
WordPiece (a subword method in the same spirit as BPE)
BPE (via SentencePiece), numbers split into individual digits, unknown characters fall back to bytes

list: **Byte-level BPE**: GPT-2 points out that doing BPE over Unicode characters would require more than 130,000 initial characters alone, while common BPE vocabularies have only 32,000 to 64,000 entries; switching to **bytes** gives an initial vocabulary of just 256 and can represent any string, including Chinese and emoji. It also forbids BPE merges across character categories, otherwise it would learn a pile of duplicate tokens like dog. dog! dog?.

**Numbers split into individual digits**: the LLaMA paper splits every number into individual digits and doesn't explain why. The common understanding is that this keeps digit tokenization more regular—you don't get irregular chunks like “1234” split into “12” and “34”—and is friendlier for arithmetic.
**Tokens determine what a model “sees”**: context length, per-token pricing, and the odd mistakes models make when counting letters or doing arithmetic all trace back to how the text is tokenized.

blocks.p: The next piece in this thread returns to vision for another foundational building block: **residual connections** (ResNet), which let networks with over a hundred layers train at all.

sections.h: Check yourself: did you really get it?

quiz.q: With BPE, what happens to an English word never seen during training?
options: It is split into learned subword pieces—at worst into single letters—so it can always be represented.
It has to be looked up in a dictionary.
quiz.why: At test time, split the word into characters, then apply the learned merge rules in the order they were learned. As long as the characters have been seen, it can always be represented—that is exactly what an “open vocabulary” means.

quiz.q: Why not simply use single characters as the vocabulary and eliminate unknown words entirely?
options: The text would become very long (about 5.5 times the whole-word baseline in Table 1), computation would grow, and the model would need to pass information across much longer distances.
quiz.why: Encoder-decoder computation is at least linear in sequence length. BPE finds a compromise between vocabulary size and sequence length: a vocabulary of just over 60,000, with text only about 12% longer.

quiz.q: In the English-to-Russian experiment, what is joint BPE's advantage over learning separate BPEs for the two languages?
options: Segmentation is more consistent across the two sides; the same name is split into corresponding pieces in both languages, so the model can more easily learn to transliterate piece by piece.
quiz.why: With separate BPEs, the translation of rakfisk had an extra letter and a missing letter, because the training data segmented the two sides inconsistently. Joint BPE first romanizes the Russian into Latin letters and learns on both sides together, so segmentation stays consistent.

blocks.p: After reading this, you should be able to answer these questions:

list: What problems do word-level translation models have with rare words? Why is the back-off dictionary not enough?
What are the four steps of BPE? Why add an end-of-word symbol?
Why is the number of merges the only hyperparameter? How does it affect vocabulary size and text length?
How does BPE handle a new word at test time?
What are the advantages of joint BPE versus learning BPE separately?
Why can shrinking the vocabulary and using more subwords sometimes be better?
What problem does GPT-2's byte-level BPE solve?
